title: ML-driven microburst shepherd & isolation handoff PRD (wip)
content:
Objective:
Design an ML-driven microburst admission and isolation handoff system ("Shepherd") for Dedicated pools that reduces cold-start tail latency, limits noisy-tenant impact, and provides transparent, auditable soft-fallbacks to hosted/model-variant lanes. This is a practical PRD sketch — focused on engineering constraints and rollout safety rather than long-term research proofs.

Background / motivation:
- We get frequent short, high-concurrency spikes (microbursts) from a small subset of tenants which cause cascading latency SLO violations across other tenants in the same slab.
- Current heuristics (static burst credits + simple prewarm) either under-utilize hardware or allow noisy neighbors to monopolize slots during short windows.
- ML forecasts from usage traces show signal patterns 15–90s prior to many microbursts (request rate slope + token-length burst + customer cron fingerprints). We can leverage that to: prewarm selectively, route early, and apply soft isolation proactively.

Key concepts / components:
1) Forecast Fusion Service (FFS):
   - Real-time lightweight model that ingests per-tenant request rate slope, historical burst periodicity, region-level load, and calendar features. Outputs a short-horizon probability that tenant will produce a microburst in next T seconds (configurable T, default 60s).
   - Runs at edge or regional aggregator to minimize cross-region telemetry.

2) Microburst Shepherd (admission controller):
   - Uses FFS score + current queue depth + per-tenant credit balance to decide: prewarm (spin ephemeral slice), route to hotlane (dedicated low-latency slab), or softly tunnel to hosted/fallback variant.
   - Applies probabilistic sampling to avoid deterministic overreaction.

3) Soft Isolation Handoff / Delegation Voucher:
   - Delegation voucher: ephemeral token granted when a tenant is predicted to burst; allows temporary allocation of a small slice or preference in scheduler for X seconds. Voucher usage logged and billed to track economics.
   - If voucher is exhausted, Shepherd performs graded handoff: (a) increase tenant priority within private slab, (b) soft tunnel subset of requests to hosted API or cheaper quantized variant, (c) enforce short-term concurrency cap with graceful 429 with retry-after.

4) Transparent Fallback Policies and Audit Trail:
   - Each decision stores a compact decision record (tenant_id, timestamp, FFS_score, action, reason) to allow post-hoc analysis and to feed model re-training.

Operational goals / constraints:
- Maintain 99th %tile latency SLO for non-noisy tenants within same reservation pool.
- Keep end-user cost delta minimal: target <8% monthly spend increase for prewarm + vouchers under standard traffic distributions.
- Deterministic safety: never preempt running inferences mid-stream; handoff only affects admission of new requests.

Success metrics (suggested):
- 99p latency reduction for pooled tenants during top-decile microburst windows (target: 30–50% improvement).
- Number of requests tunneled to hosted variants < 2% of total requests for a tenant baseline.
- Voucher utilization rate and false positive rate of FFS (target FP < 12% at recall ~70%).
- Customer-visible degraded responses (e.g., downgraded model) should be < 0.5% of requests for paying enterprise tenants.

Telemetry and signals needed:
- Per-tenant rolling qps, token length histogram, burst frequency, recent warm cache hit ratio, per-slab concurrency, queue length, per-request latency breakdown.
- Label data: prior microburst windows, responses that were prewarmed vs not, downstream SLO violations.

Rollout plan (safe + incremental):
1) Offline: run FFS model on 3 months ingest and validate recall/precision per tenant segment.
2) Shadow mode: Microburst Shepherd makes decisions and logs actions but does not act — run for 2 weeks on one region/pool.
3) Canary: enable soft prewarm only for low-risk tenants (opt-in) and enable voucher accounting. Monitor cost and 99p latency.
4) Gradual policy activation: allow hard handoffs (tunnel) only if canary metrics pass and ops runbook verified.

Implementation notes / infra integration:
- FFS: lightweight XGBoost / tiny transformer distilled runtime; must run under 50ms per tenant evaluation and be horizontally scalable.
- Shepherd: integrate with scheduling plane in runtime (scheduler hook) and with routing layer for fallback bridging.
- Billing: voucher meter increases token counters, pin to tenant billing blob for transparency.
- Privacy: ensure feature extraction strips PII; only aggregate telemetry used in FFS.

Open questions / risks:
- Model drift: burst patterns change with customer product cycles — need continuous retraining cadence and feature monitoring.
- Incentives: tenants may intentionally pad traffic to gain more vouchers — we need fraud detection and voucher policies.
- Cost-accounting complexity: ephemeral prewarms may inflate committed GPU-hours if not reclaimed timely.
- Hard-to-test edge: simultaneous multi-tenant microbursts across regions — cross-pool coordination required.

Tactical TODOs (near term):
- [ ] DED-2147: dataset extraction for FFS training (Marcus).
- [ ] Prototype Shepherd in scheduler-hook (Ava).
- [ ] Draft runbook for soft handoff and customer communication (Priya + Diego).
- [ ] Cost simulation: run 6-month synthetic trace to estimate voucher spend (Finance + Product).

Notes to reviewers / discussion points:
- Is 60s horizon the right default? shorter horizon reduces FP but less time to prewarm.
- How should we expose vouchers to customers? UI vs. opaque internal economy? (Ops prefer UI visibility).
- Policy for enterprise customers with SLAs: we should allow a toggle to forbid tunneling to hosted entirely for specific contracts.

Appendix / quick sketches:
- Decision pseudo: if FFS_score > 0.7 and slab_queue_len > threshold and voucher_balance > 0 => grant voucher and enqueue in prewarm lane; else if FFS_score > 0.85 and voucher_balance == 0 => attempt soft tunnel then cap concurrency.
- Example ledger entry fields: tenant, time, action, prewarm_alloc_ms, voucher_used, fallback_target, observed_99p_after_action.

Links / references:
- Past experiments: github.com/redwood-inference/ops/experiments/microburst-sim (internal)
- Related product notes: confluence.redwood.ai/pages/DED-prewarm-costs

Quick brain-dump at end: lots of small tenants with periodic cron jobs could destabilize dedicated slabs; if we can shift a tiny fraction of their request surface to a best-effort hosted variant with clear audit trails and per-tenant opt-outs we can substantially improve experience for paying centralized tenants. But must guard against opaqueness and cost leakage.
